paragraph: Rama thought otherwise "Mother! After my departure, deceived by Kaikeyi and deserted by you, the king will surely die. Do not commit the sin of abandoning your consort. So long as the king lives, submission to him is an unwritten law. Do not abandon him, in his hour of need. A woman's place is beside her husband, who is her lord and master.She may neglect even her worship and prayer, but cannot disregard her duties as a wife. Why do you sorrow, when a prince as noble as Bharata who knows no path except the path of dharma, is there to serve you with the greatest devotion."
Situation/Problem_Faced: Rama is trying to convince his mother, Kausalya, to accept his exile and to remain by King Dasaratha's side, despite her profound grief and fear. He argues that her duty as a wife outweighs her personal sorrow and her desire for him to stay.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Rama emphasizes the paramount importance of a wife's duty to her husband, especially in his time of need. He appeals to Kausalya's sense of dharma (righteousness) by asserting that abandoning the king would be a sin. He also tries to alleviate her worry by assuring her that Bharata will care for her.
Outcome/Resolution: In this interaction, Rama firmly but compassionately convinces Kausalya not to follow him into exile. By appealing to her sense of duty as a wife (Patni Dharma) and highlighting the potential fatal impact on the King if she were to abandon him, Rama succeeds in preventing Kausalya from further immediate action stemming from her gri. He provides a rationale for her to remain in Ayodhya, relying on Bharata's future care as a mitigating factor for her sorrow.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.stress Management: Emotional resilience, Coping mechanisms, Crisis navigation

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Dharma (Righteous Duty - Rama's core argument for Kausalya to stay by the King)
Patni Dharma (Duty of a Wife - Rama explicitly outlines Kausalya's duties as a wife)
Seva (Service - Bharata's devotion and service to Kausalya is highlighted)
Karma (Action/Consequence - The 'sin of abandoning your consort' refers to the karmic consequence of such an action)
Tyaga (Sacrifice - Rama's own impending sacrifice and his expectation of Kausalya's sacrifice for the king)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Rama appeals to Kausalya's 'Dharma' (righteous duty), specifically her 'Patni Dharma' (duty as a wife), to remain by King Dasaratha's side. He emphasizes the 'Karma' (consequences) of abandoning her consort and highlights Bharata's 'Seva' (service) as a source of comfort. This aligns with the broader theme of 'Tyaga' (sacrifice) inherent in Rama's own exile and the expected sacrifice from Kausalya for her husband's well-being.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Rama employs rationalization and an appeal to duty to help Kausalya manage her low mood, sadness, and anxiety. He attempts to mitigate her relationship challenges with the king and Kaikeyi by emphasizing the importance of her marital role. His arguments are a form of emotional support, aimed at reducing her stress and bolstering her adherence to her responsibilities, even in the face of profound personal grief.
